e: The bishop denounced the practice as cruel.
Several countries denounced the attack as a war crime.
A neighbour denounced him to the police for hiding money.

d: to show or describe something in words or pictures
e: The mural depicts the town's long history.
The novel depicts village life in the nineteenth century.
The film depicts him as a hero, which many people dispute.

d: to prevent someone from having something they need
e: The prisoners were deprived of sleep.
The illness deprived him of the chance to play again.
Many children there are deprived of clean water.

d: to get something from a source, or come from it
e: The word derives from an old Latin root.
She derives great pleasure from teaching young children.
Most of our income is derived from online sales.

d: to officially name or choose for a purpose
e: This area is designated a nature reserve.
They designated the room as a quiet study space.
He was designated team captain for the whole season.

d: to stop someone doing something by making them afraid
e: High fines are meant to deter speeding.
Bad weather did not deter the fans from queueing all night.
Bright lights around the house deter burglars.

d: to give time or effort entirely to something
e: She devotes her weekends to volunteering.
He devoted his whole life to studying ancient languages.
The last chapter is devoted to the author's childhood.

d: to identify an illness or problem after examining it
e: Doctors struggled to diagnose the illness.
She was diagnosed with diabetes at the age of forty.
The mechanic quickly diagnosed the fault in the engine.

d: to make a liquid weaker, or to reduce an effect
e: The syrup should be diluted with water.
Dilute the paint a little or it will be too thick.
Too many changes have diluted the original message.

d: to throw away something no longer wanted
e: Please discard any out-of-date medicine.
He discarded his old phone as soon as the new one arrived.
The team discarded the idea after testing it once.

d: to make known information that was secret
e: The report failed to disclose key facts.
The company refused to disclose how much it paid him.
She finally disclosed the truth to her family.

d: to make someone lose confidence or give up
e: Don't let one failure discourage you.
The long climb discouraged half the group from continuing.
High prices discourage people from buying new cars.

d: to hide the true appearance or nature of something
e: He could not disguise his disappointment.
The thief disguised himself as a delivery driver.
A little sugar disguises the bitter taste of the medicine.

d: to reject an idea, or to remove from a job
e: She dismissed the idea as impractical.
Don't dismiss his advice just because he is young.
Two managers were dismissed after the scandal.

d: to get rid of something unwanted
e: Please dispose of the batteries safely.
The factory was fined for disposing of waste in the river.
He disposed of his old furniture before moving abroad.

d: to mix fully into a liquid; to end formally
e: Sugar dissolves quickly in hot tea.
Stir until the powder has completely dissolved.
The partnership was dissolved after ten years.

d: to change something so it is no longer accurate
e: The report distorted what she had said.
Cheap speakers distort the sound at high volume.
Fear can distort the way we remember events.

d: to take someone's attention away from what they are doing
e: Loud music distracts me while I work.
He kept checking his phone, which distracted the whole class.
She told a joke to distract him from the bad news.

d: to separate and go in different directions
e: Their opinions began to diverge sharply.
The path diverges just after the bridge, so keep left.
The film diverges from the book in the final scene.

d: extreme, sudden and having a strong effect
e: The company took drastic measures to cut costs.
There has been a drastic drop in visitor numbers.
Don't do anything drastic until you have slept on it.

d: to live somewhere; to think or talk about too long
e: Try not to dwell on past mistakes.
The speaker dwelt on the risks for almost an hour.
Few people now dwell in these mountain villages.

d: feeling extremely happy and excited
e: She was ecstatic when she heard the news.
The fans were ecstatic after the last-minute goal.
He gave an ecstatic shout when his name was called.

d: to start something new; to board a ship or plane
e: They embarked on an ambitious new project.
At fifty he embarked on a completely different career.
Passengers embarked at noon and the ship sailed at two.

d: to surround completely; to include with a letter
e: Please enclose a copy of your receipt.
A high wall encloses the entire garden.
I have enclosed my CV with this application.

d: to meet or experience something, often unexpectedly
e: We encountered several problems along the way.
I encountered an old classmate at the airport yesterday.
Her first encounter with the sea was at the age of ten.

d: to make people obey a rule or law
e: The police must enforce the new rules.
Nobody enforces the speed limit on this quiet road.
Schools should enforce the ban on phones consistently.

d: to improve the quality, value or interest of something
e: Travel can greatly enrich your understanding.
Compost enriches the soil and helps plants grow.
The new arrivals enriched the culture of the whole city.

d: to happen immediately after something else
e: A heated argument ensued after the vote.
The lights went out and total chaos ensued.
In the days that ensued, nobody mentioned the incident.

d: to attract someone by offering something appealing
e: Low prices entice shoppers into the store.
They enticed him away from his job with a huge salary.
The smell of fresh bread enticed us inside.

d: to name things one by one in a list
e: She enumerated the reasons one by one.
The report enumerates every fault found in the building.
He began to enumerate his complaints on his fingers.

d: changing suddenly and without any regular pattern
e: His driving was dangerously erratic.
The heating is erratic, so some rooms are freezing.
Her performance this season has been brilliant but erratic.

d: to become more serious, intense or expensive
e: The dispute quickly escalated into violence.
Housing costs have escalated over the past five years.
Try to calm him down before things escalate further.

d: unusually good, or very rare and unusual
e: She showed exceptional talent from a young age.
The service in that hotel was truly exceptional.
Late entries are accepted only in exceptional circumstances.

d: a short passage taken from a longer text
e: He read an excerpt from his new novel.
The magazine printed a short excerpt of the interview.
We listened to an excerpt from the symphony in class.

d: to keep out or leave out deliberately
e: The price excludes tax and delivery.
They excluded him from the group chat after the argument.
The study excluded anyone under eighteen.

d: to show a quality clearly, or to display publicly
e: The patient exhibited unusual symptoms.
The child exhibits a real talent for drawing.
Her paintings are being exhibited in a small gallery.

d: to force someone officially to leave a place
e: Two students were expelled for cheating.
He was expelled from the country within a week.
The party expelled three members for breaking its rules.

d: the total amount of money, time or energy spent
e: Public expenditure rose sharply last year.
We must cut expenditure on travel and equipment.
The project required a huge expenditure of effort.

d: to reach the end of a valid period
e: Your passport expires next month.
The offer expires at midnight on Sunday.
My gym membership expired and I never renewed it.

d: extremely beautiful, delicate and finely made
e: The dress was made of exquisite silk.
She wore a pair of exquisite silver earrings.
The chef served an exquisite dessert with fresh figs.

d: to invent something false; also to manufacture
e: He was accused of fabricating the whole story.
The witness had fabricated evidence to protect his friend.
The parts are fabricated in a small workshop nearby.

d: an irregular rise and fall in level or amount
e: Sudden fluctuations in price worry investors.
Big fluctuations in temperature can damage the plants.
Doctors monitored the fluctuations in his blood pressure.

d: to lose a right or possession as a penalty
e: By quitting, he forfeited his bonus.
If you cancel late, you forfeit the deposit.
The team forfeited the match by arriving two hours late.

d: impressive and difficult to deal with or defeat
e: They faced a formidable opponent in the final.
Learning the alphabet was a formidable task at first.
She has a formidable memory for names and dates.

d: the crime of deceiving people to get money
e: She was jailed for tax fraud.
The bank blocked the card after spotting credit card fraud.
The so-called doctor turned out to be a complete fraud.

d: having no chance of success; completely pointless
e: All their efforts proved futile.
It is futile to argue with him when he is angry.
They made one last futile attempt to save the building.

d: to judge or measure roughly; a measuring instrument
e: It's hard to gauge public opinion on this.
I couldn't gauge his mood from that short message.
The fuel gauge showed that the tank was almost empty.

d: a very quick and incomplete look at something
e: She caught a glimpse of him in the crowd.
I only glimpsed the number plate as the car sped past.
The interview gave us a glimpse into her private life.

d: the feeling of being thankful for something
e: He expressed his deep gratitude to the team.
She sent flowers as a small sign of her gratitude.
I owe him a huge debt of gratitude for that advice.

d: unfriendly and strongly opposed to someone or something
e: The proposal met with a hostile reception.
He gave me a hostile stare and refused to shake hands.
The plants somehow survive in that hostile desert climate.

d: modest, not proud; also simple and low in status
e: Despite his fame, he remained humble.
She is humble about her success and never boasts.
He rose from humble beginnings to run a huge company.

d: to light something up; to make a subject clearer
e: Candles illuminated the entire hall.
Street lamps illuminate the path all the way home.
Her lecture illuminated a topic I had always found confusing.

d: to put deep into liquid; to involve yourself completely
e: She immersed herself completely in the work.
Immerse the pasta in boiling water for ten minutes.
Living abroad immerses you in the language very quickly.

d: to weaken or damage how something works
e: Lack of sleep can impair your judgement.
The accident permanently impaired his hearing.
Heavy rain seriously impaired visibility on the motorway.

d: not favouring one side over another
e: A judge must remain impartial at all times.
We need an impartial observer to settle this argument.
The newspaper claims to give impartial coverage of the election.

d: to slow down or block the progress of something
e: Debris impeded the flow of the river.
Heavy snow impeded the rescue teams for two days.
Poor equipment is impeding our research badly.

d: extremely important and needing urgent action
e: It is imperative that we act now.
Booking early is imperative if you want a seat.
Speed was the imperative, so we skipped the details.

d: something that encourages you to do something
e: Tax breaks act as an incentive to invest.
Free coffee is a small incentive to arrive early.
Students have little incentive to study without clear goals.

d: to bring something unpleasant, especially cost, on yourself
e: They incurred heavy losses last quarter.
You will incur a fee if you pay after the deadline.
His remarks incurred the anger of the whole committee.

d: so necessary that you cannot manage without it
e: A good dictionary is indispensable for learners.
She has become indispensable to the whole department.
A warm coat is indispensable in this climate.

d: to persuade someone, or to cause something to happen
e: Nothing could induce him to change his mind.
They induced her to sign with the promise of a bonus.
Certain foods can induce headaches in some people.

d: to allow yourself or someone else something enjoyable
e: Once a week she indulges in a rich dessert.
On holiday I indulge my love of long lazy breakfasts.
Grandparents love to indulge their grandchildren.

d: having no skill; done very badly
e: The response to the crisis was utterly inept.
He is so inept in the kitchen that he burns toast.
Their inept handling of the complaint lost them a customer.

d: to break a law, rule or someone's right
e: The design infringes an existing patent.
The new rules infringe on our right to privacy.
He was fined for infringing the copyright of a song.

d: clever, original and cleverly designed
e: She came up with an ingenious solution.
The lock has an ingenious design that nobody can copy.
He found an ingenious way to open the jar with a spoon.

d: to live in a particular place
e: Rare birds inhabit these remote islands.
Only a few families still inhabit the old town centre.
These caves were inhabited thousands of years ago.

d: to put something inside or between other things
e: Insert the card and enter your code.
She inserted a comment in the middle of the document.
Insert the batteries the right way round.

d: to gradually put ideas or feelings into someone
e: Good coaches instill confidence in players.
My parents instilled a love of reading in me early.
The training instills discipline in every new recruit.

d: complete and not damaged in any way
e: The ancient vase was found completely intact.
The parcel arrived intact despite the long journey.
His reputation remained intact after the investigation.

d: to stop something before it reaches its destination
e: The message was intercepted before it arrived.
Police intercepted the van at the border.
He intercepted the pass and scored within seconds.

d: to explain the meaning of something; to translate speech
e: How you interpret the poem is up to you.
Don't interpret my silence as agreement.
She interpreted for the doctor during the appointment.

d: to frighten someone into doing what you want
e: He tried to intimidate the smaller boys.
Witnesses said they had been intimidated into staying silent.
Huge crowds can intimidate young performers.

d: to enter or interrupt where you are not wanted
e: I don't want to intrude on your evening.
Reporters intruded into the family's private grief.
Sorry to intrude, but there is a call for you.

d: extremely useful; too valuable to measure
e: Her advice proved absolutely invaluable.
Volunteers gave invaluable help after the flood.
That year abroad was an invaluable experience for me.

d: a complete list of goods or items in stock
e: The shop does a full inventory every month.
Our inventory of spare parts is running low.
He made an inventory of everything in the flat before moving.

d: not connected with the matter being discussed
e: That fact is completely irrelevant here.
His age is irrelevant if he can do the job well.
Please leave out irrelevant details and get to the point.

d: very generous, expensive or given in large amounts
e: They threw a lavish party for the launch.
The hotel serves a lavish breakfast with twenty dishes.
She lavished attention on her new puppy.

d: something left behind by the past or by someone
e: The war left a bitter legacy of distrust.
Her legacy is a school that still teaches hundreds of children.
He received a small legacy from his uncle.

d: not strict when punishing or judging someone
e: The judge was unusually lenient with him.
Our teacher is lenient about late homework.
Critics say the fine was far too lenient for such damage.

d: to set free from control, prison or restriction
e: The city was liberated after a long siege.
Quitting that job liberated her from constant stress.
Volunteers liberated the animals from the small cages.

d: using the exact original words or basic meaning
e: That is the literal meaning of the phrase.
A literal translation often sounds strange in another language.
He took my joke in a literal way and got upset.

d: to examine something very carefully and in detail
e: Auditors will scrutinize every line of the accounts.
She scrutinized his face for any sign of a lie.
Journalists scrutinized the minister's expenses for months.

d: careful because of possible danger or trouble
e: Be wary of deals that sound too good to be true.
The dog was wary of strangers and kept its distance.
Investors are wary after last year's losses.
